title: US defaults on debt by 2027?
description:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if the United States federal government fails to make a scheduled payment on any Treasury note, bond, or bill at any point between November 5, 2025, and December 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

If Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s, or Fitch publicly classify any U.S. sovereign debt as being in default during the qualifying period this will qualify for a “Yes” resolution. 

The resolution source will be official information from the U.S. Department of the Treasury, Standard & Poor’s, Moody’s, and Fitch.

eventMetadata.context_description:
**Traders assign a 97.3% implied probability to "No" on the US defaulting on its debt by end-2026, reflecting the timeline mismatch between projected fiscal deadlines and the market's resolution date.** The debt ceiling currently stands at $41.1 trillion following the 2025 reconciliation increase; outstanding debt subject to the limit has reached roughly $40 trillion, with projections from the Bipartisan Policy Center and National Taxpayers Union placing the statutory limit contact date between February and July 2027. Treasury extraordinary measures would then provide an additional six-to-nine-month buffer, pushing any potential X-date into 2028—well after the market closes.

Congress has raised, suspended, or revised the debt limit 78 times since 1960, consistently prioritizing avoidance of missed Treasury payments that would trigger higher borrowing costs, rating downgrades, and market volatility. Recent developments, including ongoing bipartisan discussions around further reconciliation packages and the affirmation of the AA+ rating by Fitch, reinforce expectations that lawmakers will act before exhaustion occurs. While elevated deficits near $2 trillion annually and interest costs exceeding $1 trillion create longer-term pressure, these factors do not alter the near-term path to a negotiated increase.

Realistic scenarios that could still shift odds include an unprecedented multi-month impasse coinciding with an unforeseen cash-flow shock, though historical precedent and institutional incentives make such an outcome before 2027 highly remote.
